entities.name: Quintus Sulpicius Longus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Quintus Sulpicius Longus, a scion of the distinguished Roman patrician gens Sulpicii, held the office of consular tribune in the pivotal year of 390 BC (or 387 BC, depending on varying ancient chronologies). His historical footprint is almost exclusively defined by the catastrophic Sack of Rome by the Senones Gauls under Brennus, an event that inflicted profound trauma upon the nascent Roman Republic and indelibly shaped its military and political trajectory for centuries, leaving a deep imprint on its collective memory and national psyche.

During his term as one of six consular tribunes, Roman forces suffered a crushing defeat at the Battle of the Allia on July 18, 390 BC, against the invading Gallic tribes. This ignominious rout left Rome utterly exposed, leading directly to the city's capture and extensive burning, with only the fortified Capitoline Hill managing to withstand a prolonged siege. Roman tradition, meticulously recorded by later historians such as Livy, places Longus among the besieged officials tasked with negotiating the city's ransom with Brennus, a negotiation famously punctuated by Brennus's defiant declaration, 'Vae victis!' ('Woe to the vanquished!'). While his specific actions beyond his magisterial role are sparsely documented, his presence at this juncture is undeniable.
